image_prompt.text: Prefab track chunks 100 studs long whose exit pivot matches the next chunk's origin, in five types — Empty, TrainYard, BarrierRun, TunnelSection, RampSection — weighted at random and never repeating twice in a row
Three parallel lanes each 8 studs wide, centred at X = -8, 0 and +8, running along +Z with the track continuing to the horizon
Low barriers 8 x 3 x 2 to hurdle and raised signs to slide under, each occupying one lane
Moving trains 8 x 12 x 60 closing on the player at 25 studs/sec, only in chunks whose adjacent lanes are clear for 60 studs
Stationary trains, full blockers and tunnel overhangs that end the run on contact — the stationary trains have runnable roofs, the tunnels leave a gap only at 0-4 studs height
Obstacle groups never blocking all three lanes at once, with at least 25 studs of clear space between groups at base speed, scaling up with speed

layout_placement.text: Coins in arcs, straight lines of 5-10, and curves tracing the jump arcs, rotating 90 degrees a second
Coin Magnet, 2x Multiplier, Jetpack, Super Sneakers and Hoverboard pickups, roughly one every 300 studs, weighted
A cleanup volume 200 studs behind the player recycling cleared chunks, with 6 chunks kept ahead and 2 behind

mechanics: Third-person endless runner; the character auto-runs forward and the run ends on collision
Base speed 40 studs/sec, +1.5 every 15 seconds, hard cap 110
Lane change on a 0.15s lerp, blocked at the outermost lane, allowed mid-air
Jump 0.75s airtime peak 9 studs; roll 0.6s halving hitbox height; roll cancels a jump; 0.12s input buffer before landing
Swipe detection on mobile: touch delta over 40 pixels within 0.3s, dominant axis wins
Difficulty tiers by distance: 0-500m max one lane blocked, 500-1500m max two, 1500m+ two plus faster trains and tighter gaps
Collision by spatial query each frame against a CollectionService Obstacle tag, not .Touched
Death sequence: freeze, stumble animation, camera pull back over 0.5s, Game Over UI after 1s
Near-miss bonus of 5 points within 2 studs plus a Close Call flash
Score = distance + coins x 10 + near-miss, times active multiplier; high score saved via DataStore
Camera behind and above at (0,12,-18) looking 10 studs ahead, lerp 0.15, FOV 70 to 85, shake on lane change
HUD: coins top-left, score top-centre, multiplier top-right, powerup countdown rings below; mobile is swipe-only with no buttons
Shop with cosmetic skins, permanent powerup-duration upgrades to 5 levels, and a coin-cost revive 20 studs back
Music pitch scales 1.0 to 1.15 with speed, ducked 50% on death; SFX for jump, land, roll, coin, powerup, crash, near-miss
Single player per server slot, or parallel tracks offset 200 studs on X
notes: P2 added on top of the genre's P6: stationary trains have runnable roofs and tunnels span the lanes overhead, so surfaces genuinely overhang the play route.
Every dimension in the spec is carried in text or count rather than normalised — lane width, chunk length, obstacle sizes, spacing and despawn distance are all load-bearing to the generator.
The prompt never says what the world looks like beyond train-yard fittings, so the theme is read off the trains alone.
Parallel tracks for multiple players at 200-stud X offsets would multiply the frame width; built as the single-track case.

constraints.text: Anchor every part in chunks; set CanCollide = false on all obstacles (collision handled by spatial query)
Target 60 FPS: keep loaded part count under 2000, use StreamingEnabled on the Workspace
Chunk pool: reuse instances rather than Instance.new each time; store chunk prefabs in ReplicatedStorage.Chunks

open_questions.ask: What does the world around the track look like — a modern city rail yard, an industrial back-lot, or somewhere more stylised?
Do you want the single-track version, or the parallel tracks offset 200 studs apart so several players run side by side?
Should the five chunk types look visually distinct from each other — different buildings and dressing per type — or all one continuous setting?

captured: 100-stud modular chunks with matched pivots, 6 ahead and 2 behind
five chunk types, weighted, no repeats
low barriers, high signs, full blockers, stationary and moving trains, tunnel overhangs
obstacle sets never blocking all three lanes
25-stud minimum clear space scaling with speed
five powerups roughly one per 300 studs

notes_for_us: This is the most precisely specified prompt in the batch and the handoff holds almost none of its numbers structurally — count is a single scalar per pick, so lane width, chunk length, obstacle dimensions and spacing rules all ended up inside prose text. For a P6 generator those are inputs, not flavour.

The genre route is P6 and I added P2 for runnable train roofs and tunnels over the lanes. Nothing says whether a runner's overhangs are supposed to count, and the override table only covers dropping P2, never adding it.
Roughly two thirds of this prompt is mechanics and it triaged cleanly, which is the rule working. But the mechanics array is now 16 entries of specification that no layout reader will use.

skill_gap.name: numeric spec has no structure
skill_gap.why: count holds one number per option, and this prompt supplies dimensions, offsets, spacing rules and streaming distances that a P6 chunk generator needs as parameters; all of them survive only as English inside text

image_prompt.text: Corners, gaps and blind turns the player can break the zombie's line of sight around
Wall scrambles, ledges and trusses the player can parkour up while running
Gaps and drops to clear at speed, laid out so a running player can keep momentum
A way out set into the outer edge of the space, reached by outrunning the zombie
Ramps rising and falling through the space, run up and jumped off rather than climbed

layout_placement.text: Separated start points so the player and the zombie do not begin on top of each other
The escape trigger at the far edge of the run
Where the zombie enters and the ground it chases across

mechanics: Player runs away from a pursuing zombie
Player moves 1.2x faster than the zombie
Very cool running animations for both the player and the zombie
notes: Survival leads and Obby & Platformer is named second, so Obby's genre-wide P6 does not apply. The P6 here comes from warren-looping itself, which needs zero dead ends or the chase is unfair.
The prompt never says whether the chase ends. gate-escape is emitted because a chase needs somewhere to end, and the alternative — an endless loop — is the open question.
Ramps are stated outright and have no option; carried as free text.

open_questions.ask: Is there an end to this — somewhere you escape to and the run is over — or is it endless until the zombie catches you?
Where does the chase happen — city streets and rooftops, an abandoned warehouse, or woods and fields?
Is the zombie one AI chasing you, or another player who is 'it'?

captured: player is 1.2x faster than the zombie

notes_for_us: The prompt is one sentence padded with 40 repetitions of 'very'. Stripping the padding leaves five real facts, and the skill handled it fine, but nothing in intake says what to do with emphasis — 'very very very cool' is the user telling us what matters and there is no field for it.

Survival leading and Obby second is the documented way to avoid importing Obby's P6, and then warren-looping brings P6 back anyway. The outcome is right but the reasoning path is odd enough to be worth a line in the mixing section.
Ramps appear in the Simulation physics-rig row and in no obstacle option, so a parkour prompt naming ramps has no ID for its main feature.
